newsitem.title: USA: Rights group presses U.S. to deport Haitian.
newsitem.headline: Rights group presses U.S. to deport Haitian.

text.p: A rights group urged the U.S. government on Monday to deport Haitian paramilitary leader Emmanuel "Toto" Constant back to his country to be "brought to justice for his crimes."

"It is totally inconsistent with the values of American democracy to have a known terrorist and human rights violator arrogantly parading around New York oblivious to the outcry that he be brought to justice for his crimes," Ron Daniels, executive director of the Centre for Constitutional Rights, told a news conference.

Constant, leader of the Front for the Advancement and Progress of Haiti (FRAPH), was released from a Maryland detention centre in June last year and lives in the New York City borough of Queens. Both Haitian and U.S. government officials have called FRAPH a terrorist organisation.
The Immigration and Naturalisation Service (INS) is to examine Constant's case on Aug. 8 and decide whether to review his status again in six months, grant him asylum or return him to Haiti.
Daniels said the CCR had written U.S. Attorney General Janet Reno, New York's congressional representatives, Gov. George Pataki and Mayor Rudolph Giuliani to urge Constant's deportation.

Constant fled murder charges in Haiti in December 1995, soon after U.S. forces ended three years of military government and paramilitary terror in the Caribbean country. He arrived on a tourist visa that was revoked soon after his arrival in the United States.

Constant, who was admitted working for the CIA, was released last year in exchange for dropping a civil lawsuit charging the statute under which he was held was unconstitutional. A Baltimore immigration judge had issued a deportation order against Constant in 1995.
Constant is required to report to INS offices periodically. Officials say he is "under supervision".

CCR staff attorney Jennifer Green said she believed Constant had not been deported because "I think they are concerned about what he might say on the witness stand". CCR also represents plaintiffs seeking damages against Constant for alleged abuses.
At the time of last year's ruling, the U.S. government defended its decision to allow Constant to remain in the country by saying his return would have strained Haiti's legal and political system.
